phonemes.desc: Long close [eː], the long e of Old Irish, stressed on the first syllable as in all Old Irish words; the dictionaries mark its length with the síneadh fada.
The old cn-cluster, with the c voiced to a soft velar [ɡ] before the nasal — closer to a gargled g than to the hard c of 'cat'.
Slender n [nʲ], the palatalized nasal with a light y-glide, closing on a short, unstressed final [e].

pronunciation.approximation: 'EHG-nyeh' — hold a long tense 'eh' like French été, let the c melt into a soft g before the n, and finish with a light y-glide on the n and a short final vowel.

pronunciation.note: Ecne is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the temple form is already plain ASCII. Old Irish scribes did not write vowel length consistently — the manuscripts spell the name ecne or eicne, and the fada that marks the long é is a modern dictionary normalization — so there is no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The capital alone distinguishes the restored form from the input.

domains.title: Knowledge, Wisdom
domains.subtitle: The Poet of the Hidden Meanings; the Sense That Can Be Taken but Not Held
domains.lead: Écne is Old Irish for knowledge itself — and the name of the wisdom of the Túatha Dé Danann made personal: a poet of the divine race whose dossier is a single luminous word and a place on the list. Around the name the Irish learned tradition built its whole physics of wisdom: nine hazels over the well, nuts of knowledge falling into the water, and the salmon that feeds on them — sense that can be tasted, carried, and passed on, but never dammed or owned.

cards.name: The Nine Hazels
cards.desc: The hazels of wisdom stood over the well in the Otherworld, blossoming and fruiting in a single hour, dropping their nuts into the water below.

cards.name: The Well of Wisdom
cards.desc: Connla's well, the well of Segais — the hidden source beneath the hazels, from which the rivers of knowledge flow and to which none may walk who is not called.

cards.name: The Salmon of Knowledge
cards.desc: The fish that feeds on the fallen nuts and wears their wisdom as spots — knowledge that must be caught, cooked, and tasted, never kept.

cards.name: Imbas, the Great Knowledge
cards.desc: The poet's illumination — the flash of knowing that comes unbidden, burns the thumb that touches it first, and belongs to no one for long.

mythology.lead: Écne has the thinnest dossier of any figure in this collection — no surviving tale acts him, no epithet colors him, no treasure is laid in his hand. The tradition gives a name, a word, and a seat among the poets of the Túatha Dé Danann, and then it does something stranger and more honest: it tells the myths of the thing the name means. The mythology of Écne is the mythology of knowledge itself — the well, the hazels, the salmon, and everyone who ever burned a thumb on it.

myths.title: The Name on the List
myths.text:
Old Irish écne — also written eicne — is the common noun for knowledge, wisdom, understanding, the word the glossators reach for when they mean knowing of the deepest kind. The medieval tradition also knew it as a personal name: Écne, a poet of the Túatha Dé Danann, wisdom personified and given a seat among the divine race. That is nearly all that survives — no adventure, no contest, no death-tale. The dictionaries and the handbooks, from the Dictionary of the Irish Language to MacKillop, record the figure and then fall back on the word.

The thinness is itself the tradition's comment. Irish myth is lavish with its kings and its cattle-raids, but when it personifies wisdom it falls silent on purpose: the file, the poet, was the one who knew that the highest knowledge does not submit to narrative. Écne stands in the lists the way a word stands in a glossary — complete, and pointing elsewhere.

myths.title: Knowledge from Nuts
myths.text:
Around the year 900, Cormac mac Cuilennáin's glossary — Sanas Cormaic, the first etymological dictionary in any vernacular of western Europe — took the word in hand and explained it in the manner medieval Ireland loved: écne comes from cnú, the nut, for knowledge comes from nuts. Modern philology treats the derivation as learned play rather than history, and the word's deeper etymology remains unsettled. But the gloss was never really about linguistics.

It was a compressed myth. Everyone who heard it knew the image the gloss was invoking: the hazels of wisdom and the well beneath them, the nuts that carry knowing in their shells. Cormac's etymology is the tradition folding its whole doctrine of wisdom into a dictionary entry — the sense that knowledge is something grown, ripened, dropped, and only then taken up.

myths.title: The Well and the Hazels
myths.text:
The Irish learned tradition kept the physics of wisdom exact. In the Otherworld stands a well — Connla's well, or the well of Segais — and over it grow the nine hazels of wisdom, which blossom and fruit in a single hour so that flower and nut hang together. The nuts of knowledge fall into the water, and the salmon of the well feed on them, and whoever would drink wisdom must wait for what the trees let fall.

The image runs through the medieval teaching tradition and the mythological handbooks that preserve it, and it never varies in its essentials: the source is hidden, the fruit drops on its own season, and the water carries the knowing outward into every river of the world. It is the exact opposite of a treasure-hoard. Wisdom in this tradition is not stored; it flows, and the best any person can do is stand downstream of it.

myths.title: The Salmon and the Thumb
myths.text:
The tradition's great story of wisdom received belongs to Fionn mac Cumhaill. In the Boyhood Deeds of Finn, the boy — still called Demne — comes to the poet Finnéces, who has waited seven years by the Boyne for the salmon of knowledge, the fish that fed on the nuts of the well. On the day the boy arrives, the salmon is caught at last; Finnéces gives it to Demne to cook, with one command: eat none of it.

The boy burns his thumb on the fish and thrusts it into his mouth — and the knowledge that seven years of watching could not win passes into him by accident. When Finnéces asks whether he ate of the salmon, the boy answers no, and tells the truth of the thumb; the poet, who waited longest, surrenders the fish and the gift to him. It is the tradition's perfect parable of its wisdom-word: knowledge is not inherited, purchased, or even earned by patience. It is tasted — and it goes where it will.

myths.tag: The Settling of the Manor of Tara
myths.title: The Salmon That Remembers
myths.text:
The oldest bearer of the tradition's knowledge is Fintan mac Bóchra, the survivor who outlived the Flood itself. When the nobles of Ireland disputed the divisions of Tara, the judgment had to be sought from memory deeper than any living man's — and Fintan was found at last, ancient beyond reckoning, having passed through the shapes of salmon, eagle, and hawk, remembering every wave and every king since the waters rose.

Fintan settles the manor from the store of what he has witnessed, and the tale makes explicit what the well-and-salmon complex implies: knowledge in the Irish imagination is fundamentally memory — not a set of answers but the long holding of what the world has let fall. Écne's tradition keeps both halves: wisdom flows like water, and yet somewhere, in some salmon of the well, nothing is ever forgotten.

lore.syncretism: Écne has no cross-border attestation — no Gaulish altar, no Welsh namesake, and the handbooks claim none; the figure is Irish through and through, a word given a face. But the pattern the word belongs to crosses the Irish Sea intact. The Welsh tradition keeps its own story of wisdom arriving by accident to the wrong cook: the boy Gwion Bach, set to stir Ceridwen's cauldron of inspiration for a year and a day, takes the three scalding drops of awen meant for her son, and flees through shape after shape until he is reborn as Taliesin, the radiant-browed chief of poets. The parallel with Fionn and the salmon — the helper, the burn, the unmeant gift, the shape-changed transmission — is the standard comparison in the handbooks, and it maps a shared Celtic doctrine: poetic wisdom is a substance that passes from vessel to vessel, and no one can hold it by force. Within the Irish tradition Écne's closest kin are the other masters of knowing: Brigit, whom Cormac's Glossary calls the goddess the poets worshipped; Ogma, the honey-mouthed champion of eloquence; the Dagda, Ruad Rofhessa, the Red One of Great Knowledge; and Fionn himself, the wisdom-taster of the Boyne.
lore.culturalLegacy: Écne's afterlife runs through the thing the name means rather than through the name itself. The salmon of knowledge became Ireland's emblem of learning: it crowns the crests of schools and universities, and John Kindness's great ceramic-clad Salmon of Knowledge — the Big Fish of Donegall Quay, Belfast, raised in 1999 — carries the hazel-and-well story in printed tiles across its scales, the most famous piece of public art in the city. The Boyhood Deeds of Finn, with the thumb and the salmon, entered every Irish schoolroom through Lady Gregory's retellings and the Fenian anthologies, so that the parable of wisdom tasted by accident is one of the best-known stories in the language. The old word itself faded from ordinary Irish — eolas and fios do its daily work now — but the learned tradition kept écne in the glossaries, and the revival's scholars, from Kuno Meyer onward, restored the figure to the reference books where it stands today: the Túatha Dé Danann's own personification of the sense that can be taken but not held.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Écne is the god of the thing that slips through the fingers — knowledge as water, as falling fruit, as the fish that must be eaten in the moment or not at all. Every other figure in this collection is measured by what it holds: a hammer, a harp, a hoard, a hall. Écne holds nothing, because the tradition understood that the highest sense cannot be warehoused. The hazels drop their nuts on their own hour; the well gives only to those who stand downstream; the salmon yields its wisdom to the burned thumb of a boy who was told to wait.

That is the doctrine's edge, and it has not blunted in twelve centuries. The poet Finnéces kept vigil for seven years and the knowledge went to his kitchen-boy — not as injustice, but as the nature of the gift. What Écne names is the difference between information and understanding: the first can be copied, stored, and owned; the second must happen to you. The word survives in the glossaries like a sign at the head of a river — this way to the water; bring nothing to carry it in.
lore.originalScriptNote: The normalized Old Irish form is écne (also spelled eicne in the manuscripts) — Old Irish in the Insular Latin script, with the síneadh fada marking the long é in modern dictionary normalization. Old Irish scribes wrote vowel length inconsistently, and the manuscript spellings are plain; the earlier monumental alphabet, ogham, predates the manuscript tradition and preserves no attestation of this name. The temple form Ecne follows the unmarked manuscript spelling and is already plain ASCII, with no diacritic and no distinctive letter for the restoration to recover. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered long ago in the ordinary way: ecne.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

lore.archaeology: Écne is an entirely textual figure: no ogham stone names him, no votive inscription invokes him, and Irish paganism generally left literature rather than dedications. The witnesses are manuscripts. Sanas Cormaic, the glossary that folds the word into the hazel-and-nut doctrine, is preserved in the great late-medieval Irish codices, among them the Yellow Book of Lecan and the Book of Ballymote; the Boyhood Deeds of Finn survives in late-medieval Irish manuscript tradition and was first put into modern print by Kuno Meyer in the opening volume of Ériu (1904). The material afterlife of the tradition is civic rather than ancient: John Kindness's Salmon of Knowledge — the ten-metre, tile-clad Big Fish raised on Donegall Quay, Belfast, in 1999 — is the largest monument the wisdom complex has ever received, its scales printed with the texts and images of the city's memory.
